rows.synopsis: Harriet's ambition to know and see everything may change reclusive Agatha K. Plumber's life for the better.
rows.situation: Harriet breaks her own no-school-spying rule to stake out Agatha K. Plumber, a lawyer so scared of starting her new life that she has not left her bed in months. Harriet wants to witness history, and instead gets caught by dogs in pants and thrown out, and blows every appointment Mrs. Plumber had lined up.
rows.coping: Harriet wants to quit, then quotes her own rule back at herself, life is a struggle and a good spy never quits. She deputizes Janie and Sport to rebuild the schedule (a hair emergency, a bank meeting) and walks back into the building she was thrown out of, turning a caught spy into the nudge Mrs. Plumber needed.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis does not show the dogs-in-pants capture, the rebuilt appointment chain, or that Harriet's spying is what pushes Mrs. Plumber out of bed. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet M. Welsch puts reclusive Agatha K. Plumber on her spy route and discovers the lawyer quit her job to open a doggy clothing store, then got so scared of the risk she never gets out of bed. When Harriet sneaks in to witness the big first step, the dogs spot her, the housekeeper throws her out, and the whole day of appointments collapses. A good spy never quits, so Harriet recruits Janie and Sport to rebuild the schedule, marches back into the belly of the beast, and watches Mrs. Plumber finally walk out the door toward her new life.

rows.synopsis: Harriet's new coat is perfect for her, and apparently for Marion Hawthorne too. But who will win the school's vote?
rows.situation: Harriet finds the one coat that is completely her, and Marion Hawthorne claims Harriet copied her, forcing a class vote over who gets to wear it. Harriet has never beaten Marion at anything, and half the class votes out of fear.
rows.coping: Harriet digs for proof Marion is lying about only owning one coat, then reframes the vote as bigger than the coat: a stand for Pinky Whitehead and everyone Marion pushes around. She hijacks the morning announcements, and the scared kids find they can say out loud what they never dared.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis holds the vote; the script shows the Beth Ellen rope-bell proof hunt, Harriet's torn old coat as a story, and the announcements broadcast that flips the frightened voters. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet's new navy peacoat is perfect, silent as a shadow, collar up like Jack London, until Marion Hawthorne declares it is hers and demands a class vote. Harriet digs up proof that Marion's my-search-is-over single coat is a lie with Beth Ellen's help, andBill the journalist wants more than two dings on a rope bell. Caught snooping in Marion's closet, Harriet realizes the vote is really about every kid Marion has bullied. On the morning announcements she calls the vote what it is, freedom, and the class that always obeyed Marion starts saying so out loud.

rows.episode_title: Cross My Heart and Hope Not to Dance
rows.synopsis: Janie and Harriet vow never to go to dancing school, but Harriet doesn't know that Janie actually likes dancing.
rows.situation: Harriet and Janie's sacred oath to never attend dancing school starts cracking when their mothers sign them up, and worse, Harriet discovers Janie secretly likes dancing. When the instructor insists only boys may lead, Harriet revolts, and the oath book becomes the battleground.
rows.coping: Harriet drags Sport in as keeper of the oaths to invalidate the counter-oath, then faces the real choice: keep a rule that says girls can never lead, or let the oath go. She chooses the cause over the rule, throws off the gloves, and dances the revolution with everyone, no partner rules.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is the setup only; the script shows the oath/counter-oath/counter-counter-oath machinery, the girls-can't-lead confrontation, and Janie's admission she never hated dancing, she had just never tried it. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet and Janie swore a sacred oath in kindergarten: never, ever, ever attend dancing school. Their mothers finally outflank them, and at class Harriet discovers the real betrayal, Janie is smiling and admits she actually likes dancing because she never tried it. Then Mr. Dubois rules that girls must follow because boys are bigger, and Harriet decides no oath is worth defending that. With Sport reading the oath book's fine print, the counter-oath collapses, the gloves come off, and Harriet leads a no-rules dancing revolution.

rows.synopsis: After an awful day, Harriet wants some alone time. Watching Mr. Withers' 26 cats is just what she needs...or is it?
rows.situation: Harriet has a run-everything-wrong day: no dime for the subway, broken plates, grounded, and her two best friends mad at her. She decides the answer is to be truly alone and takes the cat-sitting job at Mr. Withers's apartment with its 26 cats, shutting her friends out mid-science-project.
rows.coping: Alone in the dark with nothing to write about, Harriet learns that peace turns to loneliness fast, and when Ole Golly arrives with her worried friends, she lets them in. The team effort of catching 26 escaped cats opens Mr. Withers's shut door to his estranged brother too, and Harriet concludes the trick is letting the world in.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at the doubt about alone time; the script shows the space-mission imagination, the blackout fear, the man in the brown fedora being the brother, and the let-the-world-in conclusion. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The world has it in for Harriet, so she takes Mr. Withers's cat-sitting job and plans to be truly alone, truly at peace, as she imagines it, a lone cosmonaut with 26 cats named Bobbys, Tommys, and Geraldines. She ditches Janie and Sport mid-science-project, and the peace curdles: a blackout, cat food for dinner, nothing left to write about. When a knock turns out to be her friends worried and the feared animal-control man is really Mr. Withers's estranged brother, the cat escape turns into a neighborhood rescue, and Harriet figures out that being alone all the way is just being lonely. The trick is letting the world in.

rows.synopsis: Harriet learns about her middle initial and questions who she is. Her nanny, Ole Golly, teaches Harriet a valuable lesson about identity.
rows.situation: On new-notebook day, Harriet discovers her birth certificate records her middle name as a scribble, and what she thought was a cool mysterious M might be nothing at all. She swipes the document from City Hall, gets caught, and decides she cannot trust even her parents or Ole Golly.
rows.coping: Ole Golly takes Harriet to meet her own mother, whose naming fight (Willa versus Myrtle) has run for decades, and shows her the shelf of books behind her chosen name. Harriet discovers identity is something you write: she adopts Myrtle for a day to heal the fight, keeps Harriet M. Welsch for real, and forgives her parents because even parents make mistakes, and mistakes give you great stories.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis skims the identity lesson; the script supplies the City Hall heist, Ole Golly's mother in Far Rockaway, the Willa Cather backstory behind Willa's bookstore, and the M question mark to M period arc. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: New notebook day goes wrong when Harriet learns her official middle name is a scribble, not the magnificent M she has been signing. She swipes her birth certificate from City Hall, lands in trouble with her parents and in a sulk with Ole Golly, who responds by taking her to meet her own mother. There a decades-long name fight (Willa, invented; Myrtle, inherited) shows Harriet that names are chosen as much as given, and Ole Golly's bookshelf shows what a person can build behind the name she picks. Harriet keeps Harriet M. Welsch, but now she knows what the M stands for, and she forgives her parents, because even parents make mistakes, and mistakes make great stories.

rows.synopsis: Janie and Harriet get to meet their favorite singer, only to discover a shocking truth about his music.
rows.situation: Harriet gets VIP access to her idol Vic Lancer through her TV-producer dad, then learns the song that means everything to her was written by Louis Redd, the guitarist Vic takes credit for. The star also has stage fright and a fried-pickle demand, and the show may not go on.
rows.coping: Harriet first wants to confront Vic, then hears Louis explain the unfairness he cannot fix yet, and Janie helps her see the step-by-step reality behind her outrage. She saves the show with Ole Golly's tomato sandwich made with love, gets Louis his on-air credit, and lets the friendship catch the complicated truth together.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis names only the discovery; the script shows the backstage chaos, the fried-pickle standoff, the ventriloquist's-dummy argument, and the Janie-Harriet conversation about fairness and moving step by step. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet's dad scores her VIP tickets to Vic Lancer, the singer whose song Gone, Gone, Gone feels written just for her. Backstage she meets the real writer, Louis Redd, a road musician missing his family, while Vic barricades himself in his dressing room demanding fried pickles made with love. The pickle rescue fails, Harriet's tomato sandwich succeeds, and when Vic introduces the hit live, he names Louis as its writer. Harriet learns her idol was a ventriloquist's dummy, and that fairness sometimes arrives step by step.

rows.synopsis: Harriet really wants to win a photo competition, but it means teaming up with someone she doesn't see eye to eye with: her mom.
rows.situation: Harriet and her mom enter the Birdstravaganza photo contest hunting the ruby-crowned kinglet, her mom fishing for a museum donation from the imperious bird-watcher Iris Vanderyke. The two are too different in every habit, they bicker through the park, split up, and both fail alone.
rows.coping: Each realizes the other had the missing piece, Harriet's spy instincts, her mom's polite cocoa diplomacy, and they pool information and work the trail together. Harriet stands up to Iris when she insults her mom, and the day ends with no photo and no donation but an impossible fun time together, agreed on for next year.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis frames the contest; the script shows the molting line, the Belgium cocoa trap that softens Iris's crew, Harriet telling off Iris, the five-dollar check, and the too-different/split-up/pool-information arc. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet and her mom team up for the Central Park Birdstravaganza, her mom courting donor Iris Vanderyke for the museum's molting diorama, Harriet planning to out-spy the whole avian society and beat Iris's professional crew. They are opposites in every habit, bicker, and split up, and alone they both get lost, wet, and birdless. Pooling information brings them to the kinglet together, and when Iris insults her mom, Harriet defends her at the cost of banishment. No photo, a five-dollar donation, and the real prize: a fun day together and a rematch next year.

rows.synopsis: Sport and Harriet think it is time to get rid of their beloved stuffies, but Marion's sneaky reporting changes their minds and the narrative.
rows.situation: Test pressure turns Harriet into a leg-jiggler, and she discovers her cool-under-pressure friend Sport secretly de-stresses with hugs from Doctor Bunny. When Marion photographs them with their stuffies and threatens a front-page newsletter exposé, Harriet decides she must throw Eddie Spaghetti off Crybaby Bridge and grow up for good.
rows.coping: At the bridge neither Harriet nor Sport can let go, and the tugboat-horn coin flip says keep them. Then the friends flip the story: they confront Marion by proudly introducing Eddie Spaghetti to the whole school, kids confess their own stuffies one by one, and the teacher confiscates the camera because the Gregory School embraces differences, not mocking them.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis credits Marion with changing the narrative; the script shows the secret-protection ops (Carl Spivey bodyguard deal, Martha's Paris guide, Beth Ellen), the Ole Golly double-swear trick, and the schoolroom stuffy show-and-tell reversal. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Sixth grade pressure has Harriet jiggling her leg, and spying reveals her unshakeable friend Sport calms down the same way she does: hugging his stuffy, Doctor Bunny. Marion catches them with Eddie Spaghetti and Doctor Bunny on camera and threatens a newsletter exposé, so Harriet plans a Crybaby Bridge farewell for her toast-smelling duck. But neither friend can let go, a tugboat horn rules in the stuffies' favor, and instead of hiding they march into school and out them as stuffy huggers. One by one classmates introduce Gunther the Bear and friends, Marion's camera gets confiscated, and being a stuffy hugger becomes something to declare, not deny.

rows.synopsis: Harriet adds the Garcia family to her spy route...and discovers that someone is spying on her.
rows.situation: Harriet starts spying on the new Garcia family and their son Carlos, who vanishes every night at game-show time, and discovers Carlos has a map of her spy route with her name on it. Sure he is an international spy, then the Bodega Burglar, she steals his decoy keys, gets caught mid-theft, and runs for her life.
rows.coping: The chase ends on a rooftop where both spies finally talk instead of tail each other: Carlos was decoy-baiting the real burglar, and the Garcias and Harriet's friends have already caught the thief together. Harriet admits running away from each other less and talking more is how amazing friendships happen, and Carlos becomes the friend she wishes for.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at discovering the counter-spy; the script carries the Bodega Burglar false lead, the penny-candy key theft, the rooftop showdown, and the decoy-keys reversal that makes Carlos a hero and a friend. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet adds the newly arrived Garcia family to her spy route and notices their son Carlos disappears every night at exactly game-show time. Then she catches him spying back, with a map of her own route and her name in Spanish she cannot read. Every theory runs from international spy to Bodega Burglar, and when she lifts what look like his keys, Carlos chases her across midtown. On the rooftop the truth flips: the keys were decoy bait Carlos set for the real thief, the Garcias and Harriet's friends have already caught the burglar, and the two spies finally talk instead of tail each other. The newspaper calls Carlos a hero and names Harriet M. Welsch, M included, as the girl who helped.

rows.synopsis: On her birthday, Ole Golly revisits a list of everything she wanted to do by the age of 35, and Harriet is determined to help her complete it.
rows.situation: The day before Ole Golly turns 35, Harriet finds her childhood to-do list with items unchecked, including learn to ride a bike, and turns the birthday into a mission to finish the list in one day. Ole Golly keeps going weird and evasive, and Harriet cannot tell what the list really means to her.
rows.coping: Harriet pushes until Ole Golly admits her secret: she chickens out of anything big and scary, and she is afraid to take the risk on her bookstore dream. Harriet points to the one death-defying item Ole Golly already pulled off, helping Harriet grow up, which turns out to mean learning to ride the bike with her eyes up, looking where she wants to go, and planting the tree now.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis keeps the list frame; the script supplies the bike lesson in the park, the marry-Ole-Golly recruiting subplot, the grumpy bookstore owner's warning, and Ole Golly's confession about chickening out. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A letter from Ole Golly's mother arrives holding a list she wrote as a girl: everything to accomplish by 35, with items still unchecked, including learn to ride a bike. Harriet commandeers the birthday eve to finish the list, teaching her nanny to ride while friends scout unlikely husbands, and a discouraging bookstore owner nearly undoes the day. Then Ole Golly confesses her dirty little secret, she chickens out of big, scary things, and Harriet shows her the one practically death-defying item she already did: raising Harriet. Back on the bike with her eyes up, Ole Golly decides the second-best time to plant a tree is now, and walks into a bookstore to finally begin.

rows.synopsis: When Harriet loses her last and favorite baby tooth, she struggles with saying goodbye to her babyhood.
rows.situation: Harriet's beloved last baby tooth, General Mouthwashington, commander of her Revolutionary-War mouth games, needs to be extracted, and Harriet fights the order with stretching, second opinions, and skipped appointments, because losing the tooth feels like losing being little.
rows.coping: After a tomato sandwich turns painful, Harriet admits the fear instead of winning the argument, and Ole Golly tells her plainly that part of growing up is learning to let go. Harriet finds the courage to sit in the chair, donates the tooth to science, and keeps the general's story, since nothing is truly gone if its story lives on.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is the premise; the script shows the General Mouthwashington imagination game, the mouth-stretching and Mr. Rocque's missing teeth, the parents' parallel wedding-cake fight, and the donate-his-body-to-science ending. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet's favorite last baby tooth, General Mouthwashington of her Revolutionary-War dental adventures, is boxed in by incoming adult teeth and scheduled for extraction. She tries stretching her mouth three inches, recruiting a second opinion from a dad with missing teeth, and flat-out skipping the appointment, until a tomato sandwich finally hurts. Ole Golly tells her the truth: growing up means learning to let go. Harriet rides out with courage, sends the general's body to science to keep up the good bite, and learns that nothing is truly gone if its story lives on. Her parents, meanwhile, decide their 12-year-old wedding cake was never really about the cake.

rows.episode_title: It's My Party and I'll Spy If I Want To
rows.synopsis: The Welsch family attends a neighborhood party where Harriet is determined to find out why the Robinsons are so boring.
rows.situation: The Robinsons are moving away, and Harriet has one last party to crack the story of the dullest couple on her spy route before they vanish. Disguised in a dress, she hunts them through an adult party full of casserole rivalries, comedians, and conga lines, and stumbles into the dreaded kids' room ruled by little kids.
rows.coping: When her suspect list flies loose, Harriet ends up teaming with Pinky Whitehead, the boy she never gave a chance, and the two win the charades game that finally makes the Robinsons laugh and play. Harriet never cracks the secret story, and decides the story she found instead, the first chapter of getting to know Pinky, is better.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is the setup; the script shows the kids-room pip-squeak feeding frenzy, the casserole war, the charades partnership with Pinky, and the ending where the better story is Harriet's own new friendship. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The Robinsons, so boring they make belly button lint seem exciting, are moving away, and Harriet goes to a neighborhood party in her fiendish disguise (a dress) determined to find their true story before they escape. She survives the dreaded kids' room, narrates the adults like a nature documentary, and loses her secret-identity list. Partnered with Pinky Whitehead on charades, she discovers the couple will play when someone finally asks, and they laugh all the way to winning the casserole contest. Harriet never finds the Robinsons' secret, but she finds chapter one of a story she likes better: getting to know Pinky, favorite smells and all.

rows.synopsis: At the world's fair, Harriet meets a 14-year-old photographer who is unsure of his future but shows Harriet how to cherish today.
rows.situation: At the 1964 World's Future Fair, Harriet, future great writer, hits her first writer's block on a paper about the future, then wanders off and gets lost. She is stuck with Chuck, a sullen 14-year-old photographer stuck helping his parents work the Kodak Pavilion, and neither believes the other has a clue.
rows.coping: Chuck teaches Harriet to come back to right now: what are you experiencing now, not worrying about what happens next, and the fair starts looking different from that angle. Their make-a-picture contest unlocks them both, her class comes back for her on the Ferris wheel, and Harriet writes her paper on the present, where fear about the unknowable future gives way to the now.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis frames the meeting; the script shows Harriet's writer's block, the trash-photography angle, the what-are-you-experiencing-right-now lesson, the Belgian waffle rescue note, and the paper she finally writes about the present. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: At the 1964 World's Fair, the girl who writes everything freezes on a paper about what excites her most about the future. Lost and furious, she is dumped on Chuck, a 14-year-old photographer stuck at his parents' Kodak Pavilion who does not believe in the future at all. His cure for her doom spiral is a photographer's question, what are you experiencing right now, now, and slowly the fair turns from wall-to-wall pressure into pretzel-scented sun. A make-a-picture contest unlocks them both, her class loops back for her on the Ferris wheel, and Harriet hands in the truth: the future is a guess, but the present, and the friend who changed how she sees, is right here.

rows.synopsis: Sport joins Harriet for a local scavenger hunt. But when he brings his good-luck charm to improve their chances, Harriet is skeptical.
rows.situation: Sport brings his lucky 1943 steel penny to the Bouncing Around the Big Apple scavenger hunt for the NASA Super Ball, rubbing it before every clue, while Marion cheats in a chauffeured town car and taunts Harriet, who has never beaten her at anything. Sport's luck ledger shows the penny has been used far more than once.
rows.coping: Sport refuses to keep rubbing the penny dry, and the hunt becomes a choice between shortcuts and playing fair. Harriet swallows her pride to ride with Marion, talks her out of the car with fair-and-square competition, and they finish second, losing the ball but winning the argument that you make your own luck by believing in yourself.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is the rivalry setup; the script shows the clue trail (30 Rock, Flatiron, Original Jay's pizza, Eloise at the Plaza), the penny ledger, Janie's taxi confession, and the Super Ball's very ordinary fall back to Earth. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Sport enters the Bouncing Around the Big Apple scavenger hunt armed with a lucky 1943 steel penny, and Harriet, a skill-over-luck believer, gets to watch him activate it before every clue while Marion cheats ahead in a chauffeured town car. When Sport's penny ledger runs dry, he refuses to keep rubbing it, and Harriet faces her own shortcut temptation: riding in Marion's car. She talks Marion into finishing fair and square instead, and they lose the Super Ball honestly to Marion's team, whose prize-winning ball immediately falls back to earth like every ordinary ball. The takeaway lands on both of them: you make your own luck by believing in yourself.

rows.synopsis: While Harriet's parents are out, she and Ole Golly join Mr. Waldenstein for a movie date. But can they get home before Harriet's parents do?
rows.situation: Ole Golly starts humming, which she despises, and Harriet's spy work reveals a boyfriend, the Garcias' deliveryman George Waldenstein. Then Harriet finds an envelope addressed to Mrs. Waldenstein and a park photo with a woman and baby, and hijacks the movie date to expose the secret wife, sabotaging the one person she cannot lose.
rows.coping: The envelope turns out to be George's mother, the woman his sister and nephew, and Ole Golly lets Harriet have the whole truth: yes, one day she will leave, because Harriet is growing up, but not until Harriet is ready. Harriet apologizes to George, then races the silver stilettos home, and the bicycle shortcut fails; Ole Golly is fired for the late night out.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis sells the caper; the script carries the humming clue, the Mrs. Waldenstein false lead and its correction, the but-not-until-you're-ready promise, and the cliffhanger firing. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Ole Golly is humming, and for a woman who despises humming that can only mean one thing: love. Harriet's spying turns up deliveryman George Waldenstein, and when she finds an envelope addressed to Mrs. Waldenstein plus a park photo of George with a woman and baby, she hijacks the movie date to expose a secret wife. The wife is his mother, the baby his nephew, and Harriet, publicly humiliated, admits the real fear underneath: if Ole Golly marries, she leaves. Ole Golly promises not to go until Harriet is ready, then races the Welsches' silver stilettos home by bicycle. They lose the race, and Mrs. Welsch fires her on the doorstep.

rows.synopsis: When Ole Golly announces she and Mr. Waldenstein are getting married and moving to Montreal, Harriet tries to change her mind.
rows.situation: Ole Golly is un-fired but announces she has accepted George's proposal and a move to Montreal, leaving within days when his job starts early. Harriet runs a full mature-versus-immature audit of herself, then mounts a Town-game propaganda play full of baguette fights and lonely Shoe Gollys to make her stay.
rows.coping: When the storytelling does not work, Ole Golly gives Harriet the goodbye she came for: she taught Harriet Town so Harriet could keep telling stories without her, and it is time to start writing full, real stories the whole world can read. Harriet sits on the stoop with a splinter feeling in her stomach and decides a new feeling is just another thing to write about.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is only the resistance; the script carries the moved-up departure, the tetherball win over Marion and the sore-winner lesson, the flamboyant William James quote, and the you-must-keep-playing-Town farewell. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Ole Golly is rehired and then announces the real news: she accepted George Waldenstein's proposal, and Montreal is days away instead of next week. Harriet audits her own maturity, launches a Town-game propaganda play with baguette fights and a weeping Shoe Golly, and unleashes her anger into an unstoppable tetherball championship, which earns her first-ever win over Marion and an act-your-age lesson with it. Nothing stops the move. Ole Golly's farewell reframes everything: she taught Harriet Town so the stories could continue without her, and now Harriet must write real stories the whole world can read. The goodbye leaves a splinter feeling in Harriet's stomach, which she files as a new feeling to write about.

rows.synopsis: Harriet's dream of building a life after Ole Golly is shattered when her notebook falls into the hands of her nemesis: Marion.
rows.situation: Without Ole Golly, Harriet declares the Age of Harriet, new-coat smell energy, hot lunch, a theme song, and a Trojan Chicken pitch that finally beats Marion's play idea. But her victory comes with the onion role, and when she rehearsed new lines for the side dishes, Marion snatches her private notebook, and Harriet's dream life runs straight into her own written truths.
rows.coping: Harriet dives into character research, learning the onion from every angle (Big Onion New York, Egyptian eternity, sulfur content) and even teaching Marion a line, until the notebook theft cuts the era short. The episode ends with Harriet fleeing her classmates, who now hold everything she wrote about them.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis compresses the arc; the script shows the New Car smell bravado, the Trojan Chicken win, the side-dish alliance and rewritten lines, Ole Golly's Montreal call-up and the Beckett quote, and the notebook-snatch cliffhanger. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: With Ole Golly gone, Harriet decides she feels great and launches the Age of Harriet: chipper parents, a theme song, hot lunch, and a Trojan Chicken pitch that beats Marion's play for the first time ever. The price is the onion role, which Harriet resists, then researches like a true writer (New York's Big Onion, Egyptian onions of eternity) and eventually embraces, even leading a side-dish rebellion and rewriting Marion's script. Ole Golly calls from Montreal with a Beckett quote, I can't go on, I'll go on. Then Marion gets her hands on the notebook and Harriet's private truths about everyone in class are one public reading away.

rows.synopsis: The fallout from her private thoughts becoming public leaves Harriet fighting to repair her friendships and to get her notebook back.
rows.situation: Marion reads Harriet's notebook aloud, entry by entry, until Sport walks out and Janie defects to the Spy Catchers' Club, which hunts Harriet down her own spy route using her own notes. Harriet's defiance, buying a new notebook, writing the truth no matter what, collapses into hating herself, and even her parents confiscate the replacement.
rows.coping: Harriet tries splendid solitude, Emily Dickinson in an itchy costume, then revenge (the frog), then the truth about herself: she writes in her notebook about her own snottiness, selfishness, and taking the last slice, telling the truth about herself first. It is not an apology yet, but it points there, and Janie's offered hand meets paint spilled by Rachel on purpose.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis covers the fallout broadly; the script carries the entry-by-entry reading, the Spy Catchers using the notebook's spy route, the Emily Dickinson splendor, the frog revenge that gets her in real trouble, and the turn to writing truth about herself. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes. vibe corrected to the ratified lowercase set (was sad, which is an emotion, not a felt energy).
rows.per_story_synopsis: Marion reads Harriet's notebook to the class, one cruel truth at a time, and the fallout is total: Sport walks out, Janie joins the Spy Catchers' Club, and Harriet's own spy route becomes the map for her own manhunt. She responds with a new notebook and a vow to never quit telling the truth, then splendor, then a frog in Marion's class, until even that lands her confiscated and doomed. Alone with Emily Dickinson in her imagination, she finally turns the pen on herself: she can be snotty, selfish, and a taker of the last slice. Telling the truth about herself is not an apology yet, but it is the first honest step toward one.

rows.synopsis: With the notebook causing quite a stir, Harriet hopes a backyard trial of her peers will prove her innocence.
rows.situation: Sent to a psychiatrist, Harriet meets Dr. Wagner, who offers a notebook of her own and a deal: apologize to her friends and get it back. Harriet refuses an apology and demands a trial instead, then loses it anyway when Janie cross-examines her into saying the hurtful words to her face, and discovers being right feels like losing.
rows.coping: On the witness stand Harriet is forced to say the words out loud, and Janie answers with the lesson Ole Golly's absence left open: life is not just about truth, it is about friendship, and friends apologize when they hurt friends. Harriet wins the case on a technicality, eats nothing, and walks home telling her parents the truth, I am the onion.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis frames the trial; the script shows Dr. Wagner's spy-on-yourself assignment, the Howard Finch pinkie ring, the onion-eating punishment clause, and the I am the onion self-verdict that the finale resolves. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Harriet's parents send her to Dr. Wagner, who wins her over the only way possible, with a notebook, and sets a deal: apologize to her friends and she gets it back. Harriet would rather have justice and stages a backyard trial to prove telling the truth is no crime. But cross-examined by Janie, she is made to say the mad-scientist line to her face, and loses something no verdict can restore. She wins the case and still feels like she lost, because an onion is a stinky thing that makes people cry, just like her. The episode ends with Harriet finally understanding what she actually owes her friends, and why.

rows.synopsis: After Harriet makes an unexpected discovery, she comes up with a plan to right her wrongs.
rows.situation: The notebook returns anonymously on the night of the harvest moon, but Harriet's confidence is broken, she tells her parents she cannot be a writer because everything she writes hurts people. Ole Golly's letter delivers the correction: writing is to put love in the world, not to use against your friends, and yes, she will have to apologize.
rows.coping: Harriet apologizes to Janie first and names her jealousy, then hands Sport a friendship balance sheet he coolly audits, and finally takes the Fall Harvest stage as the onion: one by one she reads each classmate a deeper-layer truth, digging past her top layer to what she loves about them, with the honestest saved for Sport, about not rushing growing up.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis hints at a discovery; the script supplies the harvest-moon notebook return (Janie), the Ole Golly letter, the audited balance sheet, and The Onion's Lament monologue that repairs every classmate. confidence high. vocabulary normalization (2026-11-12): off-list 'hopeless' mapped to sad per the nearest-term principle; coordinated feeling proud kept.
rows.per_story_synopsis: On the night of the harvest moon, Harriet's notebook comes back to her doorstep, but her heart is not in it: she tells her parents she cannot be a writer if everything she writes hurts people. Ole Golly's letter sets her straight, writing is to put love in the world, not to use against your friends, and an apology is owed. Harriet starts with Janie and admits her jealousy, tries a balance sheet on Sport and gets the math corrected against her, and then, as the onion in the Fall Harvest play, she delivers The Onion's Lament: for every classmate, a deeper-layer truth that digs past her own anger to what she actually loves. Sport gets the last page, and Harriet quadruple swears to keep putting love in the world.
